Summary: 
Meta announced on October 22, 2025, the layoff of approximately 600 employees from its AI division, including staff from the Fundamental Artificial Intelligence Research (FAIR) lab and AI infrastructure teams, as part of a strategic shift toward a new elite unit known as the TBD Lab. Meta downplayed the exodus as normal in competitive hiring. The entire strategy emerged from a crisis: Meta postponed its Llama 4 'Behemoth' model in May 2025 due to underperformance and lost most of its original Llama team to rivals. In response, Meta launched a 'buy or poach' campaign, hiring at least eight OpenAI researchers in one week and securing a $27 billion financing deal with Blue Owl Capital to expand AI data centers. CEO Mark Zuckerberg emphasized that top researchers now prioritize minimal reporting lines and maximum GPU access, reflecting a new 'compute-first' recruitment model. Despite massive investment, Meta’s latest layoffs signal that assembling a dream team is easier than sustaining a stable, cohesive organization.

articles.title: Steve Wozniak and AI Pioneers Gather 800 Signatures to Demand a 'Pause' in Superintelligence Development
articles.summary: Prominent AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, along with five Nobel laureates, religious figures, Richard Branson, Stephen Fry, and the Future of Life Institute (FLI), have gathered 800 signatures calling for a pause in the development of superintelligence. The initiative, backed by a broad scientific consensus, argues that the current trajectory of AI advancement—driven by corporations like OpenAI, Google, Meta, and xAI—is being set without sufficient public input. According to a survey conducted between September 29 and October 5, 2025, 95% of Americans believe AI development should not proceed until it is proven safe and controllable, and only 5% support the current status quo. Anthony Aguirre, executive director of FLI, emphasized that the issue is not only technical but also democratic, stating, 'This path has been chosen by companies and the economic system that drives them, but almost no one has asked the rest of humanity if this is what we want.' Despite corporate acceleration—OpenAI’s Sam Altman expects to achieve artificial general intelligence (AGI) before 2030, and Meta’s Superintelligence Labs is actively pursuing it—experts like Stuart Russell stress the need for robust safety measures, not permanent bans, as AI could potentially cause human extinction. Yoshua Bengio asserted, 'We must ensure the public has a much stronger voice in decisions that will define our collective future.' The movement marks a pivotal moment in the global debate over AI governance, with Aguirre posing a critical question: 'Do we really want systems that replace humans? Or should we decide, while we still can, the limits of the intelligence we are creating?'

articles.title: Celebrities, AI giants urge end to superintelligence quest | Macau Business
articles.summary: Over 700 scientists, political figures, and celebrities—including Prince Harry, Richard Branson, Steve Bannon, Barack Obama’s former national security adviser Susan Rice, Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, AI researcher Yoshua Bengio, and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak—signed an open letter published by the Future of Life Institute on October 22, 2025, urging a halt to the development of artificial superintelligence. The letter calls for a prohibition on creating AI systems that surpass human intelligence until they are proven safe, controllable, and have broad public support. The initiative is endorsed by the Vatican’s AI expert Paolo Benanti and public figures like will.i.am. The call follows concerns that major AI developers, including OpenAI, are racing toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) and superintelligence, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman suggesting superintelligence could be achieved within five years. Future of Life Institute President Max Tegmark emphasized the need for regulatory frameworks before pursuing such advanced AI. Anthony Aguirre, co-founder of the institute, stated that the current corporate trajectory—prioritizing AI to replace humans—is misaligned with public desires, scientific safety standards, and ethical principles. The letter echoes a prior appeal made one month earlier at the United Nations General Assembly, which called for international agreement on AI 'red lines' by the end of 2026.
